title: Using your medicine
intro: Step-by-step guidance on how each form of gender-affirming hormone therapy is actually used — patches, gels, injections, tablets and implants — plus missed doses, storage, and how to get rid of needles and old medicines safely in Australia.

sections.h: Before anything else: your own instructions win
body: Always follow the instructions your prescriber and pharmacist give you, and the Consumer Medicine Information leaflet that comes with your product. Brands differ, and so do people.
If anything below does not match what you were told, what you were told wins. Ask your pharmacist — you do not need an appointment, and you do not need to explain why you are taking it.
sections.note: Nothing here is advice for your particular situation. It is a description of how these products are generally used in Australia.

sections.h: Putting on and changing a patch
body: Estradiol patches are changed twice a week, every three or four days. Most people pick two fixed days, such as Monday and Thursday, and stick to them [1].

The two Australian brands approve different sites, so follow the leaflet for the brand you have. Estradot goes on the abdomen [1]. Estraderm MX goes on the buttock or the lower abdomen [2]. Neither may be applied to the breast or chest tissue. Use clean, dry, hair-free skin, avoid the waistline where a belt or waistband rubs the patch off, and avoid broken or irritated skin. Move to a different spot each time, and leave at least a week before reusing one [3][1][2].

Open the pouch by tearing it — do not cut it with scissors, which can nick the patch. Peel off the backing without touching the sticky side, press the patch down firmly with your palm for about ten seconds, then run your finger around the edges [3][1].
Rotate the site every time, and leave at least a week before you use the same patch of skin again [3][1].
You can shower and swim with a patch on, though water can lift the edges. If yours lifts, a waterproof dressing over the top can help [3].
Wash your hands before and after handling a patch. Fold an old one in half, sticky sides together, before you bin it. Sticky residue comes off with a little oil or lotion.
list: Choose two set days a week and keep them
Estradot on the abdomen; Estraderm MX on the buttock or lower abdomen; never the breast or chest [1][2]
Press firmly for about 10 seconds and seal the edges
Rotate sites, and leave a week before reusing a spot
Fold used patches in half before binning them
sections.note: If a patch falls off, press it back on, or put on a new one if it will not stick, on a different clean area of skin, and keep your original change days [3][1]. If one comes off repeatedly, tell your pharmacist — the adhesive varies between brands, and that matters more during a shortage, when brands get substituted [4][5].

sections.h: Applying gel, and keeping it off other people
body: Gels and creams are applied once a day, at about the same time, to clean dry skin.

Oestrogen gel goes on different areas depending on the brand, so follow your own leaflet. Sandrena goes on the lower body or thighs, changing sides each day; Estrogel is spread over a large area of the outer arms and shoulders or the inner thighs [27][28]. Neither goes on the breasts; keep Estrogel away from the genital area and Sandrena off the face and irritated skin [27][28].
Testosterone gel (Testogel) goes on the upper arms, shoulders or abdomen, not the upper chest and never the genitals. It dries in three to five minutes; once dry, cover the area with clothing [6][7].
Wash your hands with soap and water straight after applying, every time [6][7].

Testosterone gel transfers to other people through skin contact, and that transfer is not harmless — it matters particularly for children, for partners, and for pets that sleep on or against you. Wash your hands straight after applying, let the gel dry for three to five minutes, then cover the area with clothing. Wash the application site with soap and water before close skin contact with anyone. Testogel's leaflet says not to shower or bathe for at least one hour after applying (its product information says six hours is preferable), and to leave six hours between applying and intimate contact [6][7]; Testavan's leaflet says to avoid showering or swimming for at least two hours [29], so follow the leaflet for your own brand.

If gel does get onto someone else's skin, wash that area thoroughly with soap and water [6]. Be careful with towels, bedding and shared furniture too: anything that touches the site before it is washed can carry medicine with it.
list: Same time each day, onto clean dry skin
Let it dry fully — about 3–5 minutes — then cover with clothing
Wash your hands immediately afterwards
Keep the site covered around children, partners and pets, and wash it before skin contact
Cover the area with clothing, and wash the site before close skin contact [6][7]
sections.note: If you are having a blood test to check your level, ask your prescriber when to have it: for Testogel the sample is usually taken in the morning before you apply that day's dose, and for Testavan it is taken 2 to 4 hours after applying.

sections.h: Your long-acting injection: finding the right spot
body: Testosterone undecanoate (Reandron 1000 and other brands) is 1,000 mg of testosterone undecanoate in 4 mL of oil [8]. It is a large, thick injection, and in Australia a doctor or nurse gives it. It is not a medicine you inject yourself [9][10].

The recommended site is ventrogluteal: the side of your hip, over the gluteus medius muscle, rather than the back of the buttock. SA Health's brochure on long-acting intramuscular injections recommends this site, and it is the site the clinician training package on this site teaches [12][11].

SA Health describes the side of the hip as safer than other sites, with large muscles that absorb medicine well. Injecting into the buttock carries a chance of hitting a large nerve or blood vessel, which sit close to that site [12][11].

The clinician does not guess where it goes. You lie on your side with the upper hip uncovered, or on your back with that hip bent a little. They put the heel of the opposite hand on the top of your thigh bone, point their index finger towards the bony point at the front of your hip, and run their middle finger along the rim of your hip bone. The injection goes into the middle of the V their fingers make [11].

The needle goes straight in at ninety degrees, and the 4 mL is pushed in very slowly — over about two minutes [11]. The product information is emphatic that this injection is given strictly into muscle and very slowly, because injecting an oily solution quickly is what causes problems [9][11].
Afterwards you get gentle pressure and a dressing. The site is not massaged or rubbed hard [11].
If you have had this injection into the buttock before and a clinic now gives it on the side of your hip, that is a deliberate change in practice, not a mistake.
list: Given by a doctor or nurse, into the side of the hip, not the buttock
You lie on your side with the upper hip uncovered, or on your back with the hip slightly bent
The spot is found from the bony points of your hip, every time
The needle goes in at ninety degrees and the 4 mL is injected very slowly
Gentle pressure and a dressing afterwards; no vigorous massage

sections.h: What happens at the injection appointment
body: The appointment is short, but you will be asked to stay afterwards, and that part is not a formality. You will be observed for at least 30 minutes after the injection [11][26].

The reason is a rare reaction called pulmonary oil microembolism, or POME. A small amount of the oil can reach the lungs, and it usually shows itself within minutes, typically within 30 minutes: a sudden cough, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness or feeling faint. A very rare allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is also possible [9][11][26].

A 2022 review of 29 studies covering nearly 8,000 patients found POME to be rare [13], and Australian standards say most episodes settle on their own within 30 minutes to a few hours, often without treatment [26]. Clinics keep you there because it is manageable and they want to be present if it happens — not because it is likely.
If you feel any of those things, tell staff straight away. Do not wait to see if it passes, and do not walk out to the car park.
Afterwards the site can ache for a day or two. Walking about helps, and a warm pack and simple pain relief are fine if your pharmacist says they suit you.
The usual schedule is a second dose about six weeks after the first, then one every 10 to 14 weeks [9][11]. Book the next one before you leave — that single habit prevents most gaps.

If your clinic is new to this injection, there is a free training package for health professionals on the [testosterone undecanoate page](#/medicines/testosterone-undecanoate#sec-med-9): a procedure and training guide covering the ventrogluteal site, slow injection and the observation period, a competency checklist, and an adverse event form. You are welcome to download it and take it with you.
list: Expect to be at the clinic for a while after the injection, not just for it
Stay for at least 30 minutes; the clinic will have emergency equipment ready
Tell staff immediately about sudden cough, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness or faintness
Some ache at the site for a day or two is normal
Book the next appointment before you leave — usually 10 to 14 weeks away
sections.note: Sudden cough, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness or feeling faint in the minutes after this injection are the symptoms to report on the spot. They are uncommon and they are treatable, and staff would far rather hear about it than not [9][13][11].

body: Many trans people inject testosterone themselves. In Australia that almost always means one of the shorter-acting esters — testosterone enantate (Primoteston Depot) or Sustanon — which are supplied on a private prescription [14][10].

The long-acting undecanoate injection is the exception. Australian general practice guidance states plainly that self-administration is not recommended, and that giving it under the skin rather than into muscle can cause a painful lump [10].

Intramuscular means into the muscle: a longer needle, straight in at ninety degrees. Subcutaneous means into the fat just under the skin, with a shorter, finer needle, and medicine there is taken up more slowly.

Australian prescribing guides describe the esters being given intramuscularly, and note that many people learn to do it themselves [15][10]. Some people and some prescribers use subcutaneous injection instead, but that is a decision for your own prescriber. Only inject under the skin if you have specifically been told to.

Before you do any of this at home, two things need to happen. Someone trained has to teach you in person and watch you do it at least once — TransHub puts it the same way, that injections are given by a medical practitioner, or by you or a friend who has been shown how [14]. And you should leave with a written plan: the product, the dose, the route, the site, how often, and who to ring if something does not look right.
list: Get taught in person, and show the person teaching you that you can do it before you do it alone [14]
Ask for the plan in writing — product, dose, route, site, how often, and who to call
Ask them to choose your needle and syringe sizes and write those down too; needle length in particular depends on your body
Get a script or a supply arrangement for needles, syringes and a sharps container at the same time

sections.h: Doing the injection, and what to watch for
body: Wash your hands and set out everything you need before you open anything. Use the sizes your prescriber or trainer chose for you — their instruction wins over anything on this page.
1. Check the medicine — right product, right strength, in date, and the oil clear rather than cloudy or full of particles.
2. Draw up. A glass ampoule snaps open; a rubber-topped vial gets wiped with an alcohol swab first. Draw slowly — thick oil takes its time.
3. Swap needles. Take the drawing-up needle off and put a fresh injecting needle on. A new needle is sharper and has no oil on the outside, so it hurts less [16].
4. Clear the air. Hold the syringe needle-up, tap until the bubbles rise, and press the plunger gently until they are gone and you are on your dose mark [16].
5. Clean the site with an alcohol swab and let it dry properly. Injecting through wet alcohol is what makes it sting.
6. Insert. Intramuscular is straight in at ninety degrees. Subcutaneous is shallower — pinch up a fold of skin if you are lean.
7. Inject slowly and steadily. Oil needs time to move, and pushing hard causes most of the soreness afterwards.
8. Withdraw, press with clean gauze, and cover it. Do not rub the site hard.
9. Drop the whole syringe and needle straight into the sharps container, without recapping.

Rotate your sites so no patch of skin is used twice in a row [16]. Subcutaneous injections generally go into the stomach, keeping clear of the belly button, or the thigh [16]. For intramuscular injections at home, the outer thigh is the usual site. Australian injection guidance no longer treats the buttock as a preferred site, because of how close it sits to the sciatic nerve and large blood vessels [17]. Use the sites the person who trains you shows you.
A bit of redness, some soreness, a small firm lump that softens over a day or two, and occasionally a bead of blood are all ordinary.
What is not ordinary: redness spreading or streaking away from the site, pain getting worse rather than better, pus, new blisters, or a fever. Any of those, get it looked at the same day [18].
list: Ask your prescriber or the person who trains you which syringe, drawing-up needle and injecting needle to use, and write it down [16]
Alcohol swabs, clean gauze or cotton, and a plastic bandage
A proper sharps container, within reach before you start
sections.note: If you are ever unsure part-way through, stop and ring the clinic or your pharmacist. Nobody minds the question, and it is a much better outcome than guessing.

body: Most tablets are swallowed with water at about the same time each day. Pick an anchor — brushing your teeth, the kettle going on — rather than relying on memory.

Some prescribers direct estradiol tablets to be taken sublingually, dissolved under the tongue or between the cheek and gum [19]. That changes how fast the medicine gets in and how blood levels rise and fall, which affects blood test results, so only do it if you have been told to [26].
Micronised progesterone capsules are usually taken at night [15][26].
Spironolactone is a diuretic, so it can make you pass more urine [15]. Its leaflet says to take it at the same time each day [30]; ask your pharmacist whether earlier in the day would suit you.
If you use a dose administration aid — a weekly blister pack made up by your pharmacy — ask whether your hormone medicines can be packed in it. Most tablets can.
Implants are small pellets placed under the skin during a short procedure with local anaesthetic, releasing hormone slowly over months.

TransHub describes oestradiol pellets being inserted in a procedure of about fifteen minutes, and replaced every six to twenty-four months depending on how you respond [19]. Testosterone pellets are used by a small number of people, and can only be made by a compounding pharmacy [14]. Neither is a registered, PBS-subsidised product in Australia, so both are paid for privately [14][19].

GnRH analogues used for puberty suppression are given this way too: goserelin (Zoladex) is a small implant placed under the skin of the abdomen, and leuprorelin is a depot injection. Both are given in a clinic every one to six months, depending on the product.
Aftercare is simple: keep the site clean and dry for a day or two, and expect some bruising. Contact the clinic if it becomes red, hot, painful or starts to discharge [18].
For daily medicines, the general rule is to take it when you remember, unless it is nearly time for the next one — then skip the missed dose and carry on. Never double up to catch up.
For patches, put a new one on as soon as you notice and keep your normal change days [3].
For a missed injection appointment, ring the clinic and rebook rather than waiting for the next scheduled slot.
Missing one dose is not an emergency. Missing them repeatedly is worth mentioning, without embarrassment — the fix is usually a different form, a different schedule, or a reminder that works.

If you are ever about to run out because of cost, a shortage, or an appointment you cannot get, talk to your pharmacist before you stop. Guidance is clear that established hormone therapy should be continued, not interrupted, unless there is a medical reason to stop [20].
sections.note: This is general guidance only. Some products have specific instructions — check the leaflet in your pack or ask your pharmacist.

sections.h: Storing your medicine safely at home
body: Most of these medicines are stored below 25 degrees, in a cool dry place, away from direct sunlight — not in the bathroom and not in a car [1][7].
Patches stay in their sealed pouches until you use them; gels and creams keep their caps on and stay upright; ampoules and vials stay in their carton, away from light.

A few have a time limit once dispensed or opened: Estalis patches keep for up to one month below 25°C after the pharmacy hands them over, and a Testavan pump for 60 days after it is first opened. Each medicine page gives its brand's rules [31][32].
Keep everything out of reach of children. Testosterone gel in particular should be stored where a child cannot get to it [7].
Check the expiry date when you pick up a new supply, especially if shortages have you keeping a buffer at home. Your pharmacist can confirm the storage rules for your brand.

sections.h: Disposing of needles and leftover medicine
body: Used needles and syringes are sharps, and they never go in a household bin. Put them straight into a sharps container that meets the Australian standard, or at least a rigid, puncture-proof container with a secure screw top — soft drink bottles, glass jars and cans are not safe. Pharmacies sell them [21][22].

When the container is full, take it to a disposal point: a public sharps bin, or a pharmacy, medical centre or hospital that accepts them. Councils provide many of the public bins, and requirements differ between states [21][22]. In South Australia, the Alcohol and Drug Information Service on 1300 131 340 will tell you your nearest sharps disposal outlet [23].

Unused or expired medicines — tablets, patches, gels, leftover ampoules — go back to any community pharmacy under the national Return of Unwanted Medicines program. Every PBS-approved pharmacy has a RUM bin, it is free, and you do not need to explain anything [24].

Hand them in rather than putting them in the rubbish or flushing them: the TGA advises pharmacy return precisely because domestic bins and sinks are dangerous to other people and harmful to the environment [25].
list: Sharps container: rigid, puncture-proof, screw top, kept out of reach
Full container goes to a public sharps bin, pharmacy, medical centre or hospital
In South Australia, ring 1300 131 340 for your nearest disposal point
Old medicines: hand them in at any pharmacy, free of charge
